card: Leaving Cousin in Brussels, Hegel took the diligence to Ghent on Friday morning and viewed the parts of the van Eyck altarpiece kept there. At 2 p.m. he boarded a horse-drawn canal barge, where passengers read or played whist in the cabin, and reached Bruges at 8 p.m.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The journey from Brussels to Ghent was uneventful, save for the heat in the diligence. I spent the afternoon in Ghent viewing the Ghent Altarpiece panels. Van Eyck’s light is uncanny; it feels less like paint and more like a window into a different epoch. I arrived in Bruges by canal barge at 8 p.m. The cabin was cramped, filled with men playing whist with a fervor that bordered on the religious. I watched a hand for an hour; one player’s arrogance was positively comical, though his play was sound.

Dinner was adequate, if uninspiring. I paid three francs for a modest meal and a bottle of local wine. I am tired, and the barge rocked enough to unsettle my stomach. I think of you and the boys here in the quiet of this Flemish town. The air is damp. I hope Karl is studying diligently and Immanuel is not causing trouble. I shall write again when I reach Paris.

Yours always,
G.W.F.
Y: On Friday morning I set out — my cousin remained in Brussels — on the diligence to Ghent, saw what could be seen of the Eyck painting there (of which we have the fine pieces in Berlin), and at 2 o’clock boarded the barge to Bruges on the canal (— it is drawn by horses; in the cabin one reads, plays whist, and so on); at 8 o’clock in the evening I arrived. Ghent has 70,000 inhabitants, Bruges 33,000 — in the exterior of the latter, the peculiar Dutch style of building is entirely preserved, which is already blurred and modernized in Ghent, and even more so in Brussels.

card: Hegel arrived in Kassel at 11 in the morning and spent the rest of the morning and the afternoon walking about the town. In the evening he sat down to write his wife an account of the journey so far.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I reached Kassel at eleven, sharp as a pin. The air is cool after the heat of the Rhineland, and my legs are thanking me for the walk through the old town. The architecture is heavy, but the gardens are superb. I spent the afternoon wandering the Herkules, though I confess the statues are a bit overwrought; I paid two thalers for the guide, which was a waste, as I know the history of the place better than he does.

Dinner was unremarkable—thin broth, cold meat. I paid four thalers for the room, which is dear for the quality. I am tired, but my mind is clear. I miss the smell of our library in Berlin and the sound of the boys’ laughter. Write to me soon, and tell me how the servants managed in my absence. I shall travel to Frankfurt tomorrow, if the weather holds.

Your affectionate,
Georg
Y: I also arrived in Cassel happily this morning at 11 o'clock, and after having walked about a great deal both in the morning and afternoon, I intend to spend this evening with you, my dear, and with the account of my life and travels up to now.... My journey is not progressing as quickly as I initially intended. It has gone reasonably well for me so far, and for people who have money and stick to the main road, the world is in good condition; — however, it also requires that they have good news from your family; I have departed reassured regarding you; but I cannot be entirely free of worry, and in any case I set out on the road with great reluctance, and I am really only traveling on because I am already on the journey and am supposed to be.

card: Hegel spent two afternoon hours at the Belvedere, then saw Rossini's Barber of Seville with Lablache as Figaro, Fodor as Rosina, Ambrogi as Bartolo and the newcomer de Franco. The audience applauded entrances and passages, and kept clapping after scenes until singers returned. He read a theatre paper's notice on the company. The Partheys, at his urging, attended every performance.
X: In the afternoon I spent a few more hours at the Belvedere and then attended Rossini's Figaro. What a Figaro Lablache is! What a Rosine Mde Fodor is! She is a perfect singer; what beauty, grace, art, freedom, and taste in her singing! And the excellent Lablache, what a bass! And how cheerful and freely comic, with nothing low or vulgar anywhere. When the entire chorus sings together, and the orchestra likewise rushes in fortissimo with all its might, it sounds most certainly as if he were singing solo, and this entirely without strain, without shouting, without a screaming tone. Ambrogi was also very good again as Dr. Bartolo, and then there was a new singer, de Franco. It is a whole hedge, partly of the most excellent, partly of flawless excellence. But what a part we the public take! Three to four actors are applauded each time at their first appearance, then every passage is applauded—or bravo! bravi! is called out, then after each scene they are immoderately applauded, the singer thanks and goes off, but the applauding continues with sustained strength, so that he or she is not merely clapped, but rather clapped out. At the end of the piece, however, no calling out or set phrases take place. So, repeated Party and others, one cannot see the Figaro performed anywhere else in Italy. I read today in a Viennese theater sheet that the most experienced are of one opinion that, according to their longest memory, no such Italian company has been in Vienna for 50 years, and certainly will not come again for the next 50 years. The Party people, after I had argued them into it, naturally did not miss a single performance and were collectively most delighted, even though they disparaged the Rossinian music, which sometimes also makes me bored as music.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The Belvedere in the afternoon was tolerable, though the crowds were thick. At six, I joined the Partheys for the *Barber of Seville*. Lablache as Figaro is indeed spirited, though Fodor’s Rosina lacks breath. The audience clapped until the singers returned three times; I confess I found the repetition tedious, but the Partheys, at my urging, were enchanted. We paid two florins for the seats, a fair price for the noise. Dinner at the tavern was mediocre, and I have already complained to the waiter about the wine. I read the theatre paper’s notice, which praises the newcomer de Franco highly. I am tired. Kiss the boys for me, and tell Karl he must stop writing such long letters.

Your devoted
G.W.F. Hegel

card: Hegel left Kassel by stagecoach on Saturday afternoon; the Englishman he had been travelling with stayed behind. Six passengers rode inside, three to a seat. Hegel sat facing backwards, opposite a student from Göttingen who held on to the rear seat marked number one throughout. The coach soon reached the river Lahn and followed it.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The heat was dreadful today. I sat facing backwards in the Kassel coach, a position that suits a man of my age, allowing me to observe the world receding while I watch my own face age in the glass. My companion, a Göttingen student, clutched the rear seat number one with the tenacity of a man defending a state’s constitution, refusing to yield an inch to the other passengers. It is a small, petty form of freedom, but I admire the stubbornness.

We followed the Lahn river, the water dark and sluggish under the sun. The food at the inn was thin broth and stale bread, but the wine was passable. I have sent for a change of shirts; the travel dust is becoming a nuisance. I do not know if you received my last letter regarding the printing proofs, but I suspect the typesetter is as slow as the river.

I am tired but content. Do not worry.

Your affectionate
G.W.F.
Y: Now I would have to continue my travel description. — I departed from Cassel on Saturday afternoon — my Englishman remained there, and I found myself from then on among entirely German countrymen, quite in the national spirit — and missed my beautiful, free Englishman all the more. — We were six (three on each seat), I was facing backwards — a student from Göttingen had and kept his seat No. 1 in the back, opposite me, unmoved —, we sat tightly, it was not for the best. — We soon reached the Lahn, and now followed this river constantly; beautiful, fertile

card: Hegel arrived in Metz after 3 p.m. and stayed the night. He reserved a front coupé seat on the diligence to Paris. Before the meal he walked through the town, seeing the cathedral from outside and the Moselle valley from the ramparts. Afterwards he attended the theatre, where garrison officers filled most seats, for a play and a vaudeville.
X:
My dearest Marie,

Metz is grey and damp, though the Moselle from the ramparts is enough to make a man forget the sleet. I walked the perimeter before dinner; the cathedral is grand but cold from the outside. I dined at the *Hôtel de la Poste*—the duck was overcooked, the wine passable, and I paid six francs for the privilege of being cold.

In the evening, I attended the theatre. The house was full of garrison officers, loud and smelling of tobacco, which made the *vaudeville* a farce of noise. I watched them more than the play; a certain Colonel, red-faced and blustering, seemed to think his applause could alter the script. It was tiresome.

I have secured a front coupé seat for tomorrow’s diligence to Paris. It will be a long drive, and I shall need my snuff.

How are the boys? I trust Ludwig is behaving in his studies. I miss your quiet company and the smell of our library more than I care to admit.

Yours,
G.W.F.
Y: At this moment, after 3 p.m., I arrive here; I could immediately depart for Paris at 5 o'clock; but according to my usual system, I intend to rest again. So I am, in fact, in France! Evening. I have already had myself registered in the Lafitte diligence in the Coupé; that is the front compartment of the carriage; there are three boxes one behind the other; the middle one is called l'interieur and the rear one Cabriolet; the Coupé has 3 seats side by side, facing forward, and is closed with windows, not open, like the so-called Cabriolets on our express post coaches. Before dinner I briefly viewed the city somewhat, the cathedral from the outside and especially the view from a part of the rampart, which is most charming; the valley, through which the Moselle flows, bounded by gentle hills, wider, richer in buildings and villages, and more attractive than the surroundings of Dresden. Since Metz is a significant fortress, the garrison is numerous. After dinner I went to the theater, which was full of officers; hardly a dozen women and civilians; List against List, — also in Germany on the theater, — and then a Vaudeville, all nonsensical — and very cold — stuff, but played and spoken with such liveliness that I understood hardly a word, especially from the wretched singing.

card: In the evening Hegel attended Mozart's Marriage of Figaro, performed by the Italian company: Lablache as Figaro, Fodor as Susanna, Dardanelli as the Countess and Donzelli as the Count. His seat was nearer the stage than on his first visit. The Kleins had extended their stay over Sunday to attend this performance.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The Italian company is here, and the air in the opera house is thick with perfumes and tobacco. We took our seats near the stage, thanks to the Kleins who extended their stay just to sit with us. Lablache’s Figaro is a marvel of agility, though Dardanelli’s Countess sings with a sweetness that makes one forget her lack of power. Donzelli is adequate. The music is still the same, but the execution is sharper.

We dined at the Hofkeller. The wine was cold and the bread stale, but the company was good. I paid a small fortune for the ticket, which I regret, but I am glad I came.

Karl writes that his health is improving; I hope he is not overworking his eyes. The heat here is oppressive. I am tired.

Your loving husband,

G.W.F.
Y: To bring this to a close, I was in the evening—where?—at Mozart’s *The Marriage of Figaro*. The Kleins stayed on Sunday for that reason. I had to admit to myself that the Italian voices in this more restrained music did not seem to have as much opportunity to develop their brilliant runs, which had been so sweet to hear; but in themselves, with what perfection were the arias, duets, etc., especially the recitatives, delivered—the latter are entirely the artist’s own natural creations. Lablache, what a Figaro! Fodor as Susanna—she would indeed have had to be more beautiful and taller for this role. Signora Dardanelli as the Countess; I sat closer to the stage this time than the first time I saw her—what a beautiful woman, a lovely Italian head, and a calmness, nobility in posture and action—very lovely, beautiful decorum—I almost fell into your situation and would have fallen in love with this woman! She is in fact most charming. Donzelli as the Count—compared rather unfavorably to her; such situations are not good for him.

card: In the evening, after writing to his wife, Hegel took the coach to Breda. There he viewed a tomb monument ascribed to Michelangelo, showing a count and his wife in alabaster lying on a black slab, while four standing figures, among them Julius Caesar, Hannibal and Regulus, support a second slab above them at the corners.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Breda just as the light was failing, having taken the evening coach from here. The air was cool, a relief after the Dutch heat. I was shown a tomb monument here, ascribed to Michelangelo, though I suspect the attribution is more wishful thinking than fact. It features a count and his wife in alabaster on a black slab, supported by four standing figures at the corners: Julius Caesar, Hannibal, and Regulus. It is a curious mix of pagan virtue and domestic repose. The composition feels heavy, the stone dark, yet there is a quiet dignity to the dead couple that surpasses the stiff, heroic posturing of the living figures above them. I paid the keeper two guilders to see it, which I think was fair.

I am tired. The food in the coach was mediocre, but the wine passable. I hope the boys are behaving themselves in Berlin. Write to me soon.

Your loving,
G.W.F.
Y: That evening, after I had written to you, I took the carriage to Breda, where I saw the magnificent work by Michelangelo—a mausoleum. Six life-sized figures of white alabaster: a count and his wife, lying in death, and four figures: Julius Caesar, Hannibal, Regulus, and a warrior standing bent over at the four corners of the black stone on which they lie, carrying on their shoulders a similar black stone—a magnificent, spirited work by the greatest master.

card: After a day in Kassel with the Beers, Hegel took a hired coach to Marburg and briefly called on Suabedissen. In Wetzlar he spent an afternoon and evening with Schulz's family; next morning Schulz showed him the town and saw him onto the 10 a.m. mail coach. He reached Koblenz the previous day and took a bath before writing.
X: I have just come from the bath and am writing to you hastily, as the post leaves at 3 o'clock and lunch is approaching. — You can see from the date and the bath taken that I have already advanced about 80 miles and am taking my cure very seriously. — I have first to give you the further report of my journey, which is rather simple. Mr. and Mde Beer will have already told you, before receiving this letter, about the pleasant day we spent together in Cassel, despite the bad weather... The express post only left Cassel on Tuesday evening, so I traveled with a hired coach on Monday the 21st from Cassel to Marburg — without any noteworthy incident; in the evening I was still able to visit Hofrath Suabedissen, Professor of Philosophy, in that bumpy little nest, but he had a whole hedge of female relatives with him, so that I set off again immediately. On Tuesday I drove to Wetzlar, where I first visited Schulz, who lives outside the city in the garden, after dinner; he and his wife had a heartfelt joy over my visit; they are all very healthy and looking well — the children, my godchildren, who were almost sickly, are all very strong and well; the garden is on a hill, and has some buildings lying about 30 steps up the slope; I had to stay with him in the afternoon and evening until 10 o'clock. In the morning Schulz came to me, showed me around the little that was worth seeing, and stayed with me until I boarded the express post at 10 o'clock. — He is with body and soul engaged in very interesting studies; his conversation was very instructive to me; the whole family lives quite happily... Yesterday I arrived in Koblenz at 10 o'clock; the express post from there to Trier leaves already tomorrow; that was too early; I will therefore only depart with it on Monday, — to Trier in one day. Had I been able to calculate it, I could have asked you to write to me in Trier, where I — and that on my birthday — could have received a letter from you; I will drink to your well-being and happiness on that occasion. — Now a heartfelt kiss and greeting, likewise to the boys. In Paris I no longer understand German. — Write to me a lot from Berlin — about you and other things... Greet the friends, Privy Councillor Schulze in particular.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The Rhine is a fine sight, though the heat is stifling. I reached Koblenz yesterday, took a bath to cool off, and have been writing to you since. The journey through Kassel with the Beers was pleasant enough; they are a decent sort, if a bit stiff. Marburg was a quick stop to see Suabedissen—he is older now, and his mind, while still sharp, moves with a certain slowness that reminds me of our own aging. In Wetzlar, Schulz’s wife made an excellent dinner. The wine was good, the bread fresh, and the conversation light. I paid two thalers for the coach to Koblenz, which I consider fair for the distance, though the driver was a fool who nearly lost a wheel on the cobblestones.

Karl and Immanuel must be in their studies. Tell them to keep their heads down and their spirits up. Ludwig is quiet, I hope. I am tired but content. The air here is thick, but the view from the castle is worth the climb.

Yours,
G.W.F.

card: Hegel had attended a three-act ballet in Paris about a sleepwalker who is found asleep in a nobleman's bedroom and later seen crossing a roof with a lantern; only the first act was danced, the rest mimed. On the previous day he visited Saint-Cloud, on the Seine outside Paris.
X: What is there to say about the ballet? — a subject that no one has yet thought to treat in a ballet, and which would hardly occur to anyone else — namely, a sleepwalker. In the first act, there is dancing — with all its complications; yet there is a plot. Grace, cheerfulness, agility (the corps de ballet has it too!); in the second act, a sleepwalker appears, coming through the window on a ladder with a lantern in her hand, into the master of the house’s bedroom, lies down — after having knelt and prayed (the French around me said she was a Protestant, since it is not a church in which she prays; Protestant churches are officially called temples here). — The master — out of reverence — climbs out of the same window and leaves her alone — great applause for this virtuous behavior. The third act begins with the greatest anger of the sleepwalker’s fiancé, that she was found sleeping in a gentleman’s room. The gentleman explains to him and to the entire audience that she came into his room as a sleepwalker; they do not want to comprehend or understand it; then she appears once more on the roof, strolling with the lantern and marching down from a high, dangerously collapsed wall; — reconciliation ends everything. — In the last two acts, there is no more dancing — but much grace and liveliness in the pantomime, which admittedly cannot be understandable everywhere. — Yesterday I was in St. Cloud — beautiful surroundings — on the bank of the Seine, whose curves here form almost a complete circle, enclosing the vineyard hill; before one lies Paris with its beautiful towers and domes and countless houses. —
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The Parisians have finally given me a sleepwalker. Three acts, though only the first was actually danced; the rest was mere miming, a pantomime of the absurd. A man wandering roofs with a lantern? I confess I found it less terrifying than the price of the wine at Saint-Cloud yesterday. The Seine was calm, but the water charges a premium for its stillness. I ate a decent duck, though the service was slow, and I paid three francs for the privilege of being ignored by the waiter.

Ludwig is well, though he complains of the dust. I do not know if it is the air or the wine, but my head feels light, perhaps too light. The French seem to mistake motion for life. I am tired, Marie. Do not worry; I shall rest before dinner.

Yours,
Georg

card: With his luggage already sent off through a shipping firm, Hegel spent the evening of the emperor's name day at the Italian opera. Twenty-nine singers of the Italian company, among them Fodor, Dardanelli, David, Donzelli, Rubini and Lablache, sang the anthem in unison. Rain ruled out illuminations. The house was full, and a German cast premiered an Auber opera.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The rain has drowned the illuminations for the Emperor’s name day, but the house at the Italian opera was thick as a crowd. Twenty-nine voices, including Fodor and Rubini, sang the anthem in unison. It was loud, certainly, though I confess the German premiere of the Auber work that followed was a trifle stiff. I met a friend who insists the food in the foyer is inferior to our Berlin dining, a claim I am not yet prepared to concede.

I have sent my luggage on ahead. It is strange to be so light; one feels less anchored, perhaps more like a thought in motion rather than a substance. I hope Karl is managing his studies with the requisite discipline, and not letting his imagination wander too far ahead of his logic. I shall write again from Prague.

Your loving
Hegel
Y: Still Vienna! My effects have already been handed over to the shipping agent, — some additions, — the subtractions belong to the travel expenses; — these, however, are no heathen money, but everything was spent on Christians and used for me — also a good Christian. Now, after the completion of such business, to — where? To the Italian Theatre! To — first, the popular song — as today on St. Francis’s Day. — The rainy weather, however, did not allow illuminations to appear, which otherwise would have been perhaps the only celebration of this day; I could learn nothing of any further fuss. I also celebrated this day by listening to the aforementioned song, performed on one side by Mrs. Fodor à la tête, then Dardanelli and so on, 13 in number, and on the other side by Signor David à la tête, Donzelli, also Rubini, Lablache, Ambrogi, Bassi, da Franco etc., 16 men high — although unison, but without solos, variations. So for such means not enough action, — the men in black, the ladies in white satin! The house was this time packed full, probably for Francis’s Day, also for the sake of the German Opera, which was given for the first time today, — French music performed by Germans and German women. On the one hand, because of the packed full house, I had for the first time the opportunity to see very many, i.e., several pretty ladies, and on the other hand I could notice more of the Viennese ladies on my part, because I did not have to see and hear Italians and Italian women on the stage. I also pass from that to the German Opera, i.e., the French charming music by Auber, performed by German throats! In the last act, passion comes into the voices through a French coup, and here they let themselves go, but earlier the soul of the song only comes to peeping and longing and being small-voiced. — But with the Italians there is immediately longing-free sound, and the metal of the nature from the first moment on, ignited and in motion; the first sound is freedom and passion, — the first tone immediately goes with free breast and soul blessed into the fray! — the divine Furore is from the start melodic

card: The previous evening's programme had ended with the first act of a ballet in which the German dancer Eberle appeared. This morning Hegel went early to the imperial library to view works by Raphael and Marcantonio. Viennese collections were open free on fixed days, the library daily; he tipped the attendants at each visit. The weather cleared in the afternoon.
X: Current and blessed, it penetrates and liberates every situation! Ask the Milder whether it is not so; — she herself, in happy; not Rossini’s music, is this, for her tone, sound, and action are from the house and from the beginning out of passion and soulful penetration, — You yourself also feel this, when in re-echoes or even only in memory this fullness re-echoes in you, lives on, and storms on. — It would still be worth mentioning that finally the first act of yesterday’s ballet was performed; Eberle, a German, danced excellently, though not quite the Italian manner of a Torelli, who with her admirable manners and even more her Roman physiognomy, gave me also an idea of Italian dancing. — But now from these profane observations and plays of the 5th Oct.... The weather has cleared up again this afternoon; certainly the Berliner Dittmar has predicted this, — for here first and in the local newspapers I see how much this prophet here, — where his fatherland is not, — counts; for which reason I also did not stay in Swabia, but went over Nuremberg to Berlin. To return to my dry historical relation, — this morning early to the Imperial and Royal Library, having been with Raphael and Marc Anton. What soulful delicacy, what Unica! Along with this also again a prosaic remark: — here one sees on certain days (in the Imperial and Royal Library every day) all the treasures of artistic genius — free of charge; to the serving attendants one gives perhaps a tip and I have always, even when it was not necessary, given tips, to do honor at least to the royal Prussian professorship. On the other hand, the Berlin-Potsdam dirtiness is notorious here and in the whole world! — and I, royal Professor publ. ordin. at the royal university in Berlin (and indeed Professor of the subject, namely of Philosophy, as the
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The day began early at the Imperial Library. I spent the morning with Raphael and Marcantonio, paying the usual modest sum to the attendants. The light here is distinct from Berlin’s; one must tip well to be left in peace. The weather cleared by afternoon, so I walked.

I confess I am tired. The Viennese have a habit of lingering over meals that tests my patience. I dined on a simple soup and bread; it was adequate, if uninspired. I think of Karl’s lessons at home and the quiet of our study.

I saw a performance earlier, though I do not speak well of the dancers. Eberle was there, but the German school seems to lack the true spirit of movement. It is all form without life. I shall not return.

I write this by candlelight. The ink is thick, but my thoughts are clear. I am well, though the cold seeps in. Give my regards to the boys.

Yours,
G.W.F. Hegel

card: Having left Paris, Hegel was in Brussels, staying at the house of his friend van Ghert. Madame van Ghert cut a quill pen for him, and he had a letter from his wife fetched from the post office.
X: Also Brussels! in the house of my friend Mr. van Ghert)) and with a quill that Mde van Ghert has just cut for me, and indeed in a trice, with a single press. — You see hereby that it has become serious, to renounce Paris, — which you, in your letter, which I have just had fetched from the post, — wanted to doubt would happen so soon...
Y:
My dearest Marie,

I write from van Ghert’s house in Brussels, where Madame van Ghert performed the odd trick of cutting me a quill pen herself. The ink is good, but the nib bites. I had my letter from you fetched from the post office this morning; your news of Karl’s grammar exercises is received with approval, though I suspect his Latin declensions are still a battleground.

The city is busy, the coffee strong, and the air sharp. I walked the boulevards this afternoon; the light is golden, but the pavement is uneven. I dined on a simple stew and a glass of wine, paying four francs. It was honest food. I am tired, as you might expect, but my spirits are high. The journey continues tomorrow toward the Rhine.

Tell the boys I am thinking of them, and that their father is well enough to complain about the weather.

Your loving,
G.

card: At 10 a.m. Hegel drove with Raumer and his party to Saint-Denis, whose cathedral, burial place of the French kings, was still draped in black from a funeral service, and on to Montmorency. There he rode a donkey to the Hermitage, where Rousseau once lived, and climbed the heights above the town, with Paris and Montmartre in view.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The day was warm, the dust thick. We drove with Raumer to Saint-Denis; the cathedral still hung in black for a recent funeral. A strange, heavy silence there. We pressed on to Montmorency. I took a donkey to the Hermitage, Rousseau’s old spot. The animal was stubborn, but the view from the heights was grand—Paris and Montmartre stretching out below like a map.

Raumer is talkative, full of French politics, but he listens well when I speak. We dined at a small inn; the wine was decent, the bread heavy. I paid five francs for the ride and supper. My legs ache, but the mind is clear.

You asked of the books I sent. They should be there by next week. Tell Karl his father thinks him too hasty in his essays on ethics; let him read more history. I miss your quiet room and the sound of the children.

I am tired. Sleep well.

Your G.W.F.H.
Y: I wrote the above yesterday morning — at 10 o’clock I drove with Raumer and his company to St. Denis and Montmoreney. There is the famous cathedral, the burial place of the Kings of France, — it was still hung with black inside from a funeral service the previous day — in Montmoreney there is an estate, called the Hermitage, where Rousseau lived for a time?), and therefore — there are many small relics (there), also a rose bush that he planted — it is frequently visited in a pilgrim-like manner and on donkeys — (also by me with such eagerness) — . Montmoreney lies high and one ascends the higher heights behind it, — one has Paris at a distance of two hours, Montmartre and the large, rich plain dotted with villages and country houses before one. — It is beautiful around Paris, fertile, varied, — no wonder that so much life is lived in the country. This evening I am going to the Italian Opera to hear the Pesaroni — highly praised — in the morning still to the Gallery in the Louvre.

card: Hegel was going back to the Louvre gallery on its last open day before an exhibition of living painters, to meet Raumer and Panofka, whom he had met there the previous day; some days earlier he had walked through it with Cousin. At the Théâtre-Français he had seen Alzire, L'École des maris, and Emilia with Mlle Mars and Mlle Leverd.
X: The painting gallery is in the Louvre, — a straight, long hall, vaulted at the top — both sides hung with paintings; — a passage, almost endless, a quarter of an hour long; I had gone through it quickly with Cousin a few days ago, yesterday I wanted to begin the more thorough studies or views, when it turned out that exactly yesterday and today there is still time, — from tomorrow the museum (i.e. the collection of paintings and also the antiquities) is closed for preparation for the painting exhibition of current masters; — there is a great wealth and famous pieces by the noblest masters, which one has seen a hundred times in engravings, present; — by Raphael, Correggio, Leon. da Vinci, Titian and so on, — I am going back again in half an hour, to find Raumer!) and Panofka, whom I met there yesterday, and to make an appointment with them for this afternoon, it is Sunday and church fair in St. Cloud (i.e. fishing in Stralau)?) ; Cousin advises against going; instead there is horse racing at the Champ de Mars. — Raumer has an audience with Mlle Mars today at noon; he must be with all the actresses); Cousin finds it ridiculous to go to her, — to Talma or Mde Pasta, — if they were still here — he would have taken me. By the way Mlle Mars; in the theater I have of course also already been — in the French one twice, — once Alzire by Voltaire and l'école des maris by Moliere — so from the most famous pieces, — the other time in Emilia, tragedy after W. Scott, — an Emilia has Mlle Mars, — then Mlle Leverd (Queen Elizabeth) played, — especially the Mars very charming and noble, of course with peculiarity; one understands Mlle Mars and Leverd every word 7); they play, as the men in general also, much more restrained, with much less pathetic raging than our actors and actresses, — the men are mediocre, Lafond the most famous after Talma, almost like a butcher; — the French are generally calmer and more definite in expressing their feelings than we are, especially you; how often do I say to you, you should say and treat the matter without feeling, yet your liveliness often suits you quite nicely!
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The air in Paris is thick with dust and ambition. I spent the afternoon at the Louvre, walking the long halls with Raumer and Panofka. It is the last day before the gallery opens to the living painters, a strange inversion of value, but the old masters still hold the ground. The light in the afternoon was poor, but the shadows in the corners gave the canvases a certain depth that the midday sun strips away.

We dined at a small table near the Seine; the wine was acceptable, the service tedious. I paid four francs for a meal that offered little more than sustenance, though the view of the river was a fair compensation. I have read your last letter; Immanuel’s progress with his Latin is noted, though I fear his attention to detail is still lacking. A boy who does not master the small rules has no business claiming the large freedoms.

I am tired. I shall take my snuff and rest.

Your affectionate
G.W.F. Hegel

card: Heavy rain began overnight and lasted through Sunday into the next morning. Hegel rested on Sunday morning; after lunch, despite the rain, he took a carriage to the Augarten and on to Nussdorf. Along the road he saw a large pear tree, its fruit already harvested, in blossom again, and he enclosed two of its blossoms in his letter.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The rain here has been a veritable deluge, soaking the city from Sunday into today. Yet I insisted on the carriage to the Augarten, and thence to Nussdorf, for a mind that sits still too long grows rust. The air is thick, but the walk was good.

Look at the enclosed petals. I stopped by a great pear tree on the road; the fruit was picked days ago, yet there it was, in full blossom again. It struck me as a strange defiance of the order of things, as if the tree had forgotten its own history. I picked two for you.

I dined at a small inn in Nussdorf. The wine was ordinary, the bread hard, but the company—two young men from the University—was lively. They spoke of the new laws with a certainty that borders on arrogance, but one has to listen to see where the spirit is turning.

Tell the boys the rain does not stop the world, only the lazy. I am tired, but content.

Your loving,
G.W.F.
Y: But now it began to rain terribly at night, all through Sunday and still this morning! What is this to become! Yet one must not give up hope. On Sunday morning I was glad that it was raining so hard—I had to rest once— but after dinner I had myself driven to the Augarten and to Nußdorf, despite the weather, on the way to which I saw a pear tree, as large as a pear tree can be, covered with blossoms; it has already borne fruit; I enclose here a little blossom, one for you, the other for those who themselves have blossomed from this land, as a sign of how greatly I recognize and value the excellence of such soil. — How the Augarten and Nußdorf are, I have provisionally gathered from this and found them very beautiful...

card: The spell of fair weather in Vienna ended. That morning the Kleins left the city; during their stay they and Hegel had done little sightseeing together but had met at meals. Hegel planned to remain a few more days to see places he had not yet visited.
X: The fine weather is now past, but the pleasant days in Aranjuez are not quite over, for I shall spend a few more here; there is still much that I do not know. But to consider this, and what I already know, more exhaustively, a few weeks would certainly not have been enough. — This morning the Kleins are leaving from here; although it was hardly possible for us to go about and see things together much, we did see each other at table, and it was a very pleasant company.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The fair weather finally broke this morning, and the Kleins have departed for their journey. We met at breakfast at 9, where I paid six Kreuzer for a decent roll and coffee. Their daughter is pleasant enough, though her father speaks with that distinct, nasal Viennese affectation that I find exhausting. We did little sightseeing together; we simply sat.

I walked alone to the Karlskirche this afternoon. The light was grey, but the architecture is imposing. I spent an hour there, thinking, as I often do, about how the stone must have been laid before the idea was fully formed. It is a strange tension, but the building holds.

I am tired. The hotel bed is stiff, and I paid two Florins for the privilege. I hope the children are well and that Ludwig is not disturbing your peace. I shall stay three more days to see the Prater.

Your loving
Georg

card: Hegel and his companions drove to an abattoir and also saw the Bourse, Montmartre, which overlooks the city, and the palace of the Chamber of Deputies. At 5:30 p.m. he dined with Cousin and Fauriel, editor of the modern Greek folk songs. Some days earlier he had dined with Mignet, Thiers, Mustoxidis and Fauriel.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The Paris heat is a beast, but the evening air on Montmartre was glorious. We visited the abattoirs today; a grim spectacle of industry, yet one must see the machinery of the city. We also inspected the Bourse and the Chamber of Deputies. The latter is grand, but I confess the former held more interest.

Dined at 5:30 with Cousin and Fauriel. Cousin is as brilliant and insufferable as ever; he speaks of history as if he invented it. Fauriel, the Greek song editor, is charming and ate with great enthusiasm. The food was excellent, the wine even better, and the bill, though stiff, was worth it for the conversation. Mignet and Thiers were absent, but their absence was felt.

I hope the boys are well and that Karl’s studies in logic are progressing without too much fuss. I miss your quiet, but the road is long.

Yours,
G.W.F.
Y: You notice that I do not write about Paris with such fire and enthusiasm as I did from Vienna, and that you have communicated much to the friends; that may be so, but everything I write is too fleeting to be capable of much communication. You must take into account that my ill health has caused me to lose much time, and then that everything is so enormously vast and sprawling that one must be externally quite vigorous to encompass more, and must stay here longer to come into deeper contacts and penetrations. It is a most interesting ground, but a few weeks are only enough to get out of the stupor and into the habit of all the brilliant and manifold things. Today, for example, we drove to an abattoir, i.e., a slaughterhouse—in which city in the world would I drive to a slaughterhouse?—but this is one of the curiosities that Paris owes to Napoleon, as it does to a hundred other great things. Then we were on the Montmartre, where one overlooks the wealth of houses in Paris and the splendid, fertile, lively surroundings; also in the Palace of the Chamber of Deputies. We saw the Stock Exchange, still laid out by Napoleon, beforehand, what a temple! At half past six o’clock I dined with Cousin and Fauriel (the editor of the Greek songs, which have also been translated into German). A few days ago we dined together with Mignet, Thiers, Mustoxidis, Fauriel, and so on; in short, one must be in Paris for half a year to become more familiar with everything for which one takes a deeper interest, and, as said, through habit to lose all interest in what is striking and worth seeing for the first period. Cousin has often laughed at me when I saw and found remarkable what the conscience of a traveler and the Manual of the Foreigner prescribed to see.

card: Hegel spent the day in Cologne, looking at the Rhine and the many large two-masted vessels on it, and visiting several churches. For Sunday morning he planned to attend a mass with music in the cathedral, probably with the young Counts Stolberg and their longtime tutor, Dean Kellermann, and to leave for Aachen that afternoon.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The Rhine at Cologne is a different beast from the stream near Berlin. The river is wide, grey, and swollen with commerce. I counted twelve large two-masted vessels today, each one a testament to the practical spirit of the West. I walked the streets, the air thick with the smell of fish and coal smoke.

I visited the cathedral; the interior is impressive, though the light is gloomy. I am to attend mass tomorrow morning with the young Counts Stolberg and their tutor, Dean Kellermann. Kellermann speaks with the confidence of a man who has never been contradicted. He believes the constitution grows from the soil, not from Parisian pamphlets. I am to leave for Aachen this afternoon. The innkeeper charged me two thalers for a room that smells of damp wool and yesterday’s onions.

I hope Karl is doing well in his studies. Obedience is the first lesson; I miss seeing him learn to listen before he speaks.

Your affectionate,
G.W.F.H.
Y: This is my day's work, — of course, I have also seen the Rhine, the endless row of large two-masted ships on it, and a few more churches. Tomorrow morning, Sunday — probably in the company of the young Counts of Stolberg and Dean Kellermann, their teacher for many years, who was present at Stolberg's death — I will still see the cathedral with a musical mass and other things, and then depart for Aachen tomorrow afternoon.

card: In Aachen Hegel sat in Charlemagne's coronation chair, shown by the sexton. He spent three hours in the morning and three in the afternoon viewing Bettendorf's painting collection, with Bettendorf himself present, then walked toward Burtscheid and took a sulphur bath. Leaving by coach early Tuesday, he reached Liège around five and stayed overnight with one fellow passenger.
X: But they were covered with gold leaf, which had engraved stories on it, of which some pieces are still preserved. On this throne, 300 years after his death, Karl was found sitting, I believe, by Emperor Friedrich, with the imperial regalia put on him, the crown on his head, the scepter in one hand, and the orb in the other; these items were added to the Imperial Regalia and his bones were interred. I sat on this throne, on which 32 emperors had been crowned, as the sacristan assured me, just as well as anyone else, and the whole satisfaction is that one has sat on it. — But the main thing was that I saw the collection of Mr. Bettendorf (which is now being sold individually) for 3 hours in the morning and likewise in the afternoon, and he had the kindness to keep me company himself. In regard to Old German art, it is the counterpart to the Boisseree collection; both combined, as both gentlemen intended — purchased by the King — would represent the most magnificent thing in this sphere of art. Mr. Bettendorf does not have such large and distinguished van Eycks as Boisseree, but his Hemlings, one picture in particular, are at least as excellent as the Boisseree ones. Some of the figures in the Boisseree Hemlings, especially the Jew gathering manna, is exactly the same one who cuts the Paschal lamb on the Bettendorf picture. — But one picture by a Roger is the highest thing one can see; every particularity — some dryness that one would wish to remove even from the most excellent Eyck works — has completely disappeared here; it is as magnificently Italian as it is Netherlandish. A jewel is likewise a picture — a Deposition from the Cross with many figures, drawn by Raphael and painted by Albrecht Dürer, what loveliness, what beauty!! — A woman with a child — attributed by some to Michelangelo — is an infinitely great painting. But above all, a night by Correggio! — just as I called the Dresden one the day of Correggio, so this is the true night. What a picture! The light emanating equally from the child — Mary is dearer to me here than in the Dresden one, and she, like the surroundings in this one, smiles — everything is also cheerful — but more serious, and the darkness, as in the Correggio pictures in Sanssouci, of the later manner of this master — of the highest excellence. In the evening I still took a walk towards Burtscheid, and since the famous bath is in Aachen, I took a bath: it is hot! and full of sulphur smell. — On Tuesday morning at 7 o'clock we left Aachen and arrived in Liège around 5 o'clock; the road goes up hill, down hill, mostly on a ridge, with deeper valleys on both sides, everything green, intersected by innumerable hedges and rows of trees. Towards Liège one gets views into the beautiful Meuse valley; I was very tempted to travel from Liège up the Meuse valley via Namur to here — but I would have spent nearly two days longer, because of the curse of the carriages, and part of the journey would have been made at night, when no one sees anything. In Liège I stayed overnight with one of the travelers; the carriage on which we had arrived went straight on; among the traveling party there was just again such a flat, chatty German — a Würzburger, who also wants to be an Englishman — annoying people, as I had had one in every carriage party so far. My
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The coach was comfortable, though the roads from Aachen to here were muddy. In Aachen I spent the entire morning and afternoon at Bettendorf’s house. He is a man of good taste and no small fortune; his collection of paintings is superb, far superior to what we see in the provincial galleries of Germany. I sat in Charlemagne’s actual coronation chair while the sexton explained the mechanics of the old empire. It is a strange sensation to sit in the seat of such power, feeling the weight of history not as abstraction, but as wood and leather.

I then walked to Burtscheid and took a sulphur bath. It was hot and unpleasant, but I confess it loosened my joints, which have been stiff from the journey. I dined at the inn; the food was plain, but the wine was decent. I have paid all bills and am ready to continue.

How are the boys? I trust Immanuel is not neglecting his Latin. I am well, if tired.

Your
G.W.F.

card: Hegel reached Amsterdam shortly after noon and went directly to Dr. Besseling, to whom Mr. van Ghert had recommended him. Afterwards he visited the picture gallery, which holds paintings by Rembrandt measuring 15 to 20 feet across and 12 feet high. He did not get through the whole collection that day.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I reached Amsterdam at noon, straight to Dr. Besseling, who was gracious but busy. The food at his table was competent, if dull; I paid two guilders for the meal. Later I wandered into the picture gallery. I must confess I was struck dumb by a Rembrandt, some fifteen feet wide. It is not merely a picture; it is the very air of the city. I did not finish the collection, nor do I wish to. My eyes are tired, and the light here is flat compared to Berlin’s.

I think of the boys. I hope they are studying, not just idling. I have taken a room near the canal; the noise of the water is constant, a kind of restlessness. I am tired, but content. Write to me soon.

Yours,
G.W.F. Hegel
Y: Arrived here in Amsterdam at 12:07 o'clock, immediately went to Dr. Besseling, to whom I had been recommended by Mr. van Ghert — a very obliging man — then to the painting gallery, — here are works by Rembrandt, 15 to 20 feet wide, 12 feet high, I have not yet seen everything.

card: The day before, Hegel had travelled to Karlstein, an old castle with old paintings, about four hours away. In hot weather this morning he revisited churches and galleries, finishing his sightseeing. He lunched with the uncle's family, who then drove the party by carriage to a pleasure ground outside town. He was to dine with them again the next day.
X: Friday, September 17. Yesterday I spent the whole day on a trip to Carlstein, an old castle four hours from here, where old paintings still hang, but otherwise there is nothing to see; — this morning I visited the churches and galleries, partly repeating what I had seen before, and have finished my business, i.e., seeing the sights. Yesterday’s tour with its heat, as well as the heat this morning, had made me very weak and affected me; — lunch at Uncle’s house today restored me wonderfully. After the meal, Mr. O. took us by carriage to a very pleasant place of amusement — here all the foliage is still firm and green, although it has not rained for a long time. Tomorrow I shall dine with the same family again; I am very well with them and with their heartfelt, friendly reception...
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The heat here is oppressive, though the air is dry. Today I finished my surveys of the galleries. The lighting is poor, and the guides are tedious, but the works themselves are sufficient. At noon I dined with the von H. family. Their table was heavy, the wine flat, but they are polite enough. They drove us to the Pleasure Garden outside the city. I confess I have little patience for such public amusements; the crowds are thick and the music shrill. I sat in a shaded corner, ate a cold chicken, and paid two florins for the privilege of standing near a fountain. The uncle’s son spoke of politics with the confidence of a boy who has never had to pay for his opinions. I let him.

I hope the boys are behaving. I shall dine with them again tomorrow, then move on. Do not worry; I am well, if somewhat tired.

Your
G. W. F. H.

card: Hegel spent 9 to 11 on a third visit to the Esterhazy gallery. Prince Esterhazy, told that a Berlin professor was there, had a valet show Hegel everything, including the private cabinet. Hegel then lunched at an inn with Professor Sonnleitner, director of the antiquities cabinet, and a professor from Padua. In the evening he saw Rossini's Corradino.
X: Now this morning, for the third time, out to the Esterházy Collection; treasures to be admired without end! — one really cannot get enough of them. — The finest pieces are in the Prince’s private room, a garden room in the pavilion — next to the castle, where the great gallery is; the Prince was in this room and, as he heard me walking around, he asked who it was? — since it was not one of the public days; — he was pleased to hear that it was a Berlin professor who had already come for the third time and ordered the valet to show me everything, and as he soon drove off, I was also able to see the magnificent pieces of the cabinet once more — what a living room! — This Prince can travel a few miles from Vienna on his own land and property right up to the Turkish border. — Stayed there from 9 to 11 o’clock, — then — half an hour to go home, — changed clothes — to the Antiquities Cabinet, whose director, Prof. Sonnleitner, had invited me — he is unmarried — to lunch with him at an inn with a professor from Padua — a very learned and amiable man. We scholars are immediately much more at home with one another than with bankers, for example. — Then some walks in the city, — finally also to the Italian Opera and, as I had so much wished, Corradino il cuor di ferro, — which was melted and softened by the charming Dardanelli; — how sweetly she sang — and how David sang again with her! I did not contradict a man with whom I had entered into conversation at dinner last evening, who even went so far as to claim that Rossini’s music is music for the heart.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

I am back in my room, exhausted but content. This morning I spent two hours in the Esterhazy gallery, a third visit, but I confess the private cabinet dazzled me. The valet was courteous, though perhaps too eager to point out every crack in the plaster. I saw the Rubens, which is indeed magnificent, but the lighting here is dim; I paid two florins for the privilege of seeing it poorly.

Lunch was with Sonnleitner and a Paduan professor. The wine was good, the roast pheasant excellent, and the conversation light. Sonnleitner is a solid man, if a bit dull on the subject of Roman law. We paid three guilders each, a fair sum for the heat.

In the evening I saw Rossini’s *Corradino*. The music is intoxicating, though the libretto drags in the second act. I nearly dozed off during the recitatives, but the chorus woke me. It is a spectacle, not a thought.

You asked about the snuff; I bought a tin of the finest brand here. It is strong. I miss your quiet, and the boys’ noise. I shall write more soon.

Yours,
G.W.F.

card: Hegel stayed mostly indoors in Koblenz, where Councillor Lange was absent, then on Wednesday afternoon took a boat to Neuwied and saw the Moravian Sisters' House. Next morning he boarded the Rhine passenger boat in rain, stopped at Linz to see a painting Schulze had recommended in a hilltop church, and at Bonn called on Windischmann and his son-in-law Walther.
X: So I would have been happy to have arrived in the venerable Imperial City of Cologne.... In Coblenz, where my last letter ends, I spent the afternoon and the following morning mostly resting at home — the Consistory Councillor Lange, to whom Schulze had addressed me, was not present, — and in indecision about the weather I let the express coaches, steam packets, and other opportunities pass by; but on Wednesday afternoon it cleared up; I took a boat and went to Neuwied on the beautiful Rhine; I saw the Moravian Brethren' house; — it became too dark to go into the Prince's Brazilian collection. The most beautiful thing was the evening — beautiful moonlight shone over the Rhine, which flowed past my windows; owls, which I had never heard speak in my life, made music in it, — in the morning after 8 o'clock onto the steam packet, an improved market boat. — At first one could be somewhat on the deck, but then it became windy, cold, rainy, finally continuous, heavy, cold rain. The company was thus confined in the cabin, and there were also students in it, who were making their Rhine journey, so with the knapsack, covered with green oilcloth and with a boot sticking out on each side of it, wide new straps, — everything in order, also white, or rather yellow straw hats. So I, although with somewhat more ballast than they, also made my Rhine journey, but therefore saw less, and was inferior to them in that I could not gain the proud consciousness of making a Rhine journey. Already the rainy weather in Coblenz, — above all this Rhine journeying, had spoiled my travel, and if it had not been so far home to you, above all if I had not been afraid of the post coaches, I would have quickly arrived at your place. I travel in general only out of duty and obligation, and would have a hundred times more satisfaction and pleasure if I could divide my time between my studies and you. If you ever come with me to this Rhine, I will lead you differently; on the water one sees neither the Rhine nor the country, — the former not, for one does not see it flowing through the fields and hills, one does not have it as a part of the picture before one, which is its truly beautiful position or flow — nor the country, for one sees only the banks, their boundaries and notices at most that it might be beautiful behind them. — In Linz we went ashore, where I saw the picture recommended by my friend Privy Councillor Schulze, and that in a high-situated church, from where one overlooks the Rhine and the beautiful country. — In abominable rain we went ashore in Bonn. Here I looked for Windischmann and his son-in-law Walther), whom you know from Thibaut, — with the former, who through union in prayer with Prince Hohenlohe?) has been healed for a year of a six-year eye ailment of the kind like Jacobi's, only much worse — and is now perfectly healthy, I got along very well, and we, for the time being, were very satisfied with each other. Walther also pleased me, who remembers you with very heartfelt remembrance, and sends you friendly greetings. — This encounter refreshed me again. To this was added the clearing up of the weather, and so I set out yesterday afternoon in a better disposition.... Bonn is hawkerish, very narrow-streeted, but the surroundings, view, botanical garden — beautiful, very beautiful, but I am still rather in Berlin.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The rain in the Rhine passenger boat this morning was miserable, but the view saved it. At Linz I visited the hilltop church Schulze recommended; the painting is adequate, though the climb was stiff. In Bonn, Windischmann and his son-in-law Walther were most agreeable. Windischmann is sharp, but Walther lacks that certain *Geist* I expect in a lawyer. We drank decent wine, though the price was steep.

I am tired. The journey from Koblenz to here has worn me thin. I hope Karl and Immanuel are well, and that Ludwig is not giving the servants trouble with his temper. Tell me how the house is settled. I shall take a short walk tomorrow if the sky clears, but for now, I am exhausted.

Yours ever,
Hegel

card: Hegel travelled on to Giessen, where he spent time with the philosophy professors of Giessen and Marburg and an associate professor of theology; the Giessen professor took them out for wine. Travellers bound for Frankfurt parted from the group there. Hegel and a Jewish schoolteacher continued together along the Lahn, passing Weilburg, a former princely residence.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The day was long, but the company in Giessen was excellent. We drank local wine with the professors; I find their arguments as dry as their cellar, but their hospitality is warm. The travelers for Frankfurt departed, leaving me with a Jewish schoolmaster, a man of surprising wit and good taste. We walked the Lahn past Weilburg. The old princely residence looks neglected, a fine ruin. I paid four Kreuzer for a simple meal at a wayside inn; the bread was stale, but the river air was crisp. I am tired, but the walk did me good. I think of Karl and Immanuel only in the sense that I hope your health is steady. Do not worry about my expenses; I am managing well. The light on the water this evening was quite striking, though I have no time to paint it. I shall write again tomorrow if the post allows.

Yours,
G.W.F. Hegel
Y: Then we went to Giessen, a pleasant city and surroundings, with two nice castles in the neighborhood. Here I was with three confreres: the Giessen professor of philosophy—Snell?—the Marburg professor of the same, Creuzer?, a cousin of the Heidelberg one—and an extraordinary professor of theology, a man of striving, insight, and cultivation. But how insipid those my nearer confreres had been, I had to overlook, as the Giessen one immediately led us to wine and treated us with very good vintage. In Giessen was the parting point for those who went to Frankfurt, among whom, as we had agreed at the start, I was not, all the less as I would otherwise have spent longer in the company up to now. My young teaching colleague, the Israelite, however, stuck with me; we followed the Lahn. Weilburg has a romantic location, a beautiful, vegetation-rich, narrow valley, pleasant bends of the Lahn—and also, as a former princely residence, nice houses.
